lesson.title: methinks & Dative Survivors
lesson.subtitle: English dative fossils mirrored in German — and the dem/den/dem grid row

hook.title: The Case English Buries and German Lives In
hook.content: English keeps dative fossils the way amber keeps insects. Methinks — 'it seems TO ME'. 'Give it me' — the British phrasing where me is the receiver. 'Give it him' — Chaucer's still-living dative. Methinks' partner 'me seems' survives as 'seems to me'. German never buried the case: it is a load-bearing wall. Mir ist kalt (it is cold TO ME), Es gefällt mir (it falls well TO ME), Ich helfe dir (I help TO thee). Today you collect the fossils and set them beside their living German relatives.

footnotes.title: The dem/den/dem Row
footnotes.content: The dative article row: dem (masculine), der (feminine), dem (neuter), den (+ -n) plural. Masculine and neuter SHARE dem — and dem keeps the ancient m that the accusative softened to n (ihn, wen). English him, whom, and 'em all still wear that m.

pattern.title: Fossil ↔ Living Word
pattern.content: Fossil one: methinks = mir dünkt's: 'it seems TO me' — the experiencer dative, alive in German as Mir ist kalt, Mir ist schlecht. Fossil two: 'give it me' ↔ Gib es mir — the receiver marked by case, not by preposition. Fossil three: 'me seems' / 'seems to me' ↔ Es scheint mir. Fossil four: wham — 'give it him' ↔ Gib es ihm. The pattern: wherever English once let the pronoun alone mark the receiver, German still does — mir, dir, ihm are the entire living system, three words doing the work of English prepositions.
pattern.linguist_note: The dative experiencer is German's favorite feeling-grammar: Mir ist kalt/langweilig/schlecht — cold, bored, and bad all happen TO you. English needs 'I am' phrases; German keeps the ancient 'it is X to-me' frame.

exercises.prompt: Match each English fossil with its living German form:

matching_pairs.german: Es scheint mir (it seems TO ME)

exercises.target_answer: Es scheint mir, Gib es mir, Gib es ihm, Ich gebe es dir, das Glück, der Mut
exercises.meaning: it seems to me, give it me, give it him, I give it thee, luck, courage
exercises.explanation: Every English dative fossil has a working German relative — the case never died on the continent. Glück and Mut are plain nouns; the dative sits on the person they reach: Ich wünsche dir Glück.

exercises.prompt: Which article completes the dative row: 'mit _____ Mann' (with the man — masculine)?
exercises.meaning: mit dem Mann — with the man (dative)
exercises.explanation: Masculine dative = dem — the same m you hear in him, whom, and 'em. Wünschen (wish — the twin) hands its gift TO someone: Ich wünsche dir Glück — the wish travels dative.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich helfe _____ Frau.' (I help the woman — dative):
exercises.meaning: Ich helfe der Frau = I help the woman
exercises.explanation: Feminine dative = der — the article that does double duty as 'to the' and 'the' (feminine). The fortress adjectives wait outside the case: jung, stark, schwach, gesund — they decline only before a noun; after sein (er ist jung) they stay bare.

exercises.prompt: Fold the repeated noun phrase into its compact pronoun:
exercises.full_sentence: Ich sehe das Buch und ich gebe dem Bruder das Buch
exercises.explanation: When both objects are pronouns, the accusative thing (es) steps ahead of the dative receiver (ihm): Ich gebe es ihm.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I give it to him' (the German way — no 'to')
exercises.meaning: I give it him / to him
exercises.explanation: The dative ihm does the job of English 'to him' — the case IS the preposition.

summary.outcome: Read English dative fossils and build German dative sentences with dem/der articles.
summary.takeaway: methinks, 'give it me', 'give it him' — the dative never died in English, it just went fossil; German keeps it employed.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: mir / dir / ihm Pronoun Gym — twenty give/tell/thank drills with the receiver pronouns.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from methinks & Dative Survivors (I give it him / to him):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich gebe es ihm" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of methinks & Dative Survivors without relying on short-term echo.

mir.context_translation: Can you please help me? (literally: help to me)
mir.etymology_derivation: Dative of ich — the same ancient pronoun as English me, keeping the 'to me' meaning (mir ist kalt = it is cold to me). [wiktionary]

ihm.etymology_derivation: Dative of er — the exact twin of English him; the h dropped from speech and stayed in spelling. [wiktionary]

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

gefallen.context_translation: I like it (it falls well to me).
gefallen.etymology_derivation: ge- + fallen — 'to fall to someone' (by lot or liking), like English 'as it falls out'. Strong verb: gefiel, gefallen. [wiktionary]

glück.etymology_derivation: Probably borrowed from Old Dutch *gilukki — Wiktionary: 'Compare English luck' (a relative via Dutch). [wiktionary]

mut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *modaz — the page lists English mood as the cognate: the English d became German t (day and Tag), and courage is having the right mood. [wiktionary]

wunsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wunska — the page lists English wish among the cognates; the verb is wünschen. [wiktionary]

wünschen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wunskijana — the page lists English wish as the direct cognate, both from the wish-love root *wen. [wiktionary]

jung.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *jungaz — the twin of English young (see der Junge). [wiktionary]

stark.etymology_derivation: From Old High German stark, Proto-West Germanic *stark; the everyday English word stark, as in stark naked, is the very same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

schwach.context_phrase: Nach der Krankheit war er schwach.
schwach.context_translation: After the illness he was weak.
schwach.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German swach, Proto-West Germanic *swak; the English cousins are the dialectal word swack, meaning nimble or lively, and Scots swack. [wiktionary]

gesund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sundaz — the same root as English sound, as in safe and sound. [wiktionary]

türkisch.etymology_derivation: Türke + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Turkish. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
